detail.longDescription: In short: For the past few years, I've been building a biohacking platform called Plants Research Pro (PRP), designed to help people discover research on bioactive materials and put that research to practical use. Recently, I added a new feature to PRP which is turning out to be my favorite so far: The Chess Lab. This is essentially a set of tools and protocols for biohacking in chess, some of which you can try right now via the link -- I recommend a Single-Session Experiment, which is a 6-test protocol that lets you explore how some intervention, like coffee, might improve your cognitive function in the context of chess. - In detail: The idea for Chess Lab started about four years ago when I came across research by Prof. David O. Kennedy's group showing that sage, cocoa, and other materials can enhance some cognitive functions. If I remember correctly, the subjects were healthy young adults (possibly uni students). I really wanted to test this on myself, and since I like chess, I chose chess as my 'test platform'. I'm not gonna go into the formulation, but I tried sage alone, sage with cocoa, and sage with cocoa and milk. The third mix seemed to give me the best focus and attention (for about 4-6 h), and my rating started to climb after a few weeks. But there was an issue - I had no idea if I was simply improving naturally, or if the mixture was enhancing it. This annoyed me a little bit, and made me realize that PRP needed an N-of-1 experimentation system. After finally getting around to it, PRP's Experiments system was implemented earlier this year, while Chess Lab was added about a month ago. Both are now live, although testing and refinement are ongoing. The system also supports N>1 experiments, so can be used with a group of people as well. There are six cognitive tests and a Single-Session Experiment (SSE) to play with for free. The tests are based on those used in cognitive research, while SSE is a simple before-and-after experiment. i.e., you choose an intervention (coffee, tea, exercise, etc.), complete 6 baseline cognitive tests, apply the intervention (drink your coffee or whatever), then repeat the tests to see what changed -- all within a day (or about 1 h for simple SSEs). The results are exploratory, of course, but I think it's pretty cool that I can now do this myself, at home, without going to a university lab. But I want to make it much better. The signal-to-noise ratio is difficult to estimate, and there are several sources of error. For instance, a chessboard recall test uses positions from real games, but some pawn structures are much easier to memorize than others. I'm examining two approaches: (1) filtering games by board complexity, and (2) introducing random configurations. The thing with (2), though, is that it's less fun and measures a somewhat different aspect of cognition, but that's a story for another day. For longer experiments, I've added Chess.com statistics, including move accuracy, rating, opponent-adjusted score, etc. And if you're not sure how to set it up, you can describe what you want in plain language (e.g., 'I want to test if lemon peel can improve my chess') and an AI-powered builder will create a research-backed recipe, design the experiment, assign metrics, and select suitable cognitive tests. AI can also help interpret the statistical results. These full experiments are part of the Premium subscription. In the coming months, I'll add more cognitive tests, analytics, and some ML capability. Most importantly, I hope to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. A new Multi-Session Crossover design (repeated SSEs alternating intervention/no-intervention days, with longitudinal analysis) should help, but there'll definitely be more work needed from different angles. Anyway, if you like chess and the idea of (safely) optimizing cognitive performance with biohacking, give Chess Lab a try! I'd be very keen for feedback, bug reports, or feature suggestions. Thanks!
